posts.title: An open morning in November
posts.excerpt: On Saturday 14 November the school opens its doors from 10:00 to 12:00 for families thinking about September 2027.
posts.content:
Aozora Primary School holds its first open morning of the year on Saturday 14 November 2026, from 10:00 to 12:00. It is for any family thinking about a place for September 2027, and children are very welcome to come too.

You do not need to book. Samuel Reyes will be at the front door with a cup of tea, and Eleanor Marsh, our head teacher, will say a few words at 10:15 about how the school began in 1979 and how it works today. After that you can walk around freely.

Dates for this winter

  • Open mornings: 14 November 2026 and 16 January 2027
  • A school-in-action morning on 3 December 2026
  • Small tours on Tuesdays at 09:30, by appointment

Every classroom is open, and the class teachers are there to talk. You will see children’s paintings and writing on the walls, the library with its cushions, the music room and the garden beds. Tom Avery will take anyone who likes on a short walk around the garden at 11:00.

If you cannot come, there are other chances: a school-in-action morning on Thursday 3 December from 09:15 to 11:00, another open morning on Saturday 16 January 2027, and small tours on Tuesdays at 09:30 by appointment. The application form for September 2027 closes on 31 January 2027.

We keep the morning quiet and unhurried. Nobody will ask you to decide anything, and there is no test. Find us at 12 Linden Lane, Westbury Vale.

posts.title: Why we read aloud every day
posts.excerpt: Every class ends the day with a story, and every child reads with an adult each week. Here is why it matters to us.
posts.content:
At Aozora Primary School every class ends the day with a story read aloud, and the whole school gathers on Friday afternoons for a longer one. It is the habit we would defend most firmly if the timetable ever became crowded.

Reading aloud lets children meet words and ideas that are further ahead than they can read themselves. A six-year-old who cannot yet read a long book can still follow one, laugh at it and ask about a word. That curiosity is what makes the early work on letters and sounds feel worthwhile.

Alongside the stories, each child reads one to one with an adult every week. In Year 1 that is usually the class teacher; by Year 5 and Year 6 it is often Mei Lin Hart, who runs the school library, and children are paired with younger readers. Eleanor Marsh, our head teacher, reads with a different child each week and says it is the best part of her job.

The library has low shelves and a pile of cushions in the corner. Children choose their own book each week, and they are allowed to change their minds. A book that is put down after three pages tells us something too.

At home, ten minutes of reading together before bed does more than any worksheet. Read the same favourite again if your child asks for it. Repetition is how stories become familiar, and familiar stories are how children learn to love reading.

posts.title: The garden in October
posts.excerpt: Year 3 has dug the last of the potatoes and sown broad beans. A short note on what the raised beds teach us.
posts.content:
The raised beds behind the playground look different this month. The sunflowers have been cut down, the last potatoes are in a crate by the door and the Year 3 class has sown a row of broad beans for the winter.

Tom Avery, who teaches Year 3 and leads our outdoor learning, says October is when the garden teaches the most patience. Nothing seems to grow, and yet the children check the bed every Wednesday afternoon and write down what they see in their garden diaries. By the end of the year the diary is full of small drawings: a frosted leaf, a worm, a seedling pushing through the soil.

The garden is part of science. Children measure how tall the beans grow, test whether the soil under the hedge is drier than the soil in the open, and learn what a plant needs. It is also part of art, when they draw a seed head, and part of cooking, when a few potatoes become lunch for the class.

Outdoor afternoons happen in nearly every kind of weather, so please send your child with a coat, a hat and spare socks in their bag. Wellington boots can be kept on the pegs in the corridor.

If you have gardening books, spare pots or seedlings you would like to give, the school office will gladly pass them on to Tom.

posts.title: How we teach mathematics with your hands
posts.excerpt: Counting rods, beads and measuring jugs come before the pencil. A note for parents on how mathematics is taught.
posts.content:
In the first years at Aozora, mathematics starts with real things. Children count with wooden rods, group beads in tens, pour water between measuring jugs and build shapes. Pencil and paper come later, once the idea is clear in the hands.

The rods on the light table in the Year 1 classroom are a good example. A child places a ten-rod beside ten single cubes and sees at once that they are the same length. When we later write 10 on paper, it already means something.

Children are asked to explain how they reached an answer. A wrong answer with a clear explanation is a good place to start, because the teacher can see exactly where the thinking turned. In classes of no more than twenty, a teacher can listen to each child every day.

By Years 5 and 6 children use written methods fluently, but they still estimate first, and they still check by a second route. The rods go back in the cupboard, though they come out again when a new idea needs explaining.

At home, you can help without worksheets. Cook together and measure, play with coins, compare heights, count steps on the way to school. Ask how your child worked something out, and listen to the answer before you say whether it is right.

posts.title: Fees, bursaries and what they cover
posts.excerpt: A short, plain note on the fees for 2026-27, how they are paid and how bursaries work.
posts.content:
Families often tell us that fees are the hardest part of choosing a school to ask about, so here is a plain summary. For the school year 2026-27 the fees are 11,400 GBP for Years 1 and 2, and 12,300 GBP for Years 3 to 6, paid in three termly instalments.

Lunch is 690 GBP a year, and children eat together at long tables with their teachers. A registration fee of 100 GBP comes with the application and is not refundable. A deposit of 1,000 GBP holds a place once it is offered, and it is credited against the final term.

A reduction of 10 percent applies for brothers and sisters. We also offer a few means-tested bursaries every year. We cannot promise one, but we will look at each application carefully and in confidence.

If you would like to talk it through, Samuel Reyes in the school office will arrange a call or a meeting with Eleanor Marsh. Asking costs nothing and does not affect an application in any way.

Fees are confirmed in writing with every offer, and we tell families in good time about any change for the following year. Our wish is that nothing in your bills should come as a surprise.

posts.title: A letter to new parents
posts.excerpt: Before September: what to expect from the first weeks, from the recorder to the school choir.
posts.content:
Dear new parents, welcome to Aozora Primary School. Starting at a new school is a big step for a family as well as a child, and a few notes may help in the first weeks.

On the first morning, gates open at 08:15 and the children hang their coats on a hook with their name above it. Morning circle starts at 08:40. Please say goodbye at the gate; the class teacher will be waiting, and we will telephone you if there is any worry at all. Home time is at 15:20, and the optional club runs until 17:30.

Music is part of every week. From Year 2 every child learns the recorder, and Clara Brandt leads the school choir, which sings for parents at the end of each term. Children who have never sung in front of anyone are often the ones who surprise us most.

Please send your child with a water bottle, a coat, spare socks and wellington boots. Lunch is at 12:10 in the dining room, where everyone eats together. If your child has any allergy, tell the school office early.

You will receive a written report every term and be invited to two parent meetings a year. If you want to talk sooner, just ask the class teacher at the gate or telephone the office on +44 20 7946 0811.
